entry.title: Chicago’s Fire Inspection Gap
entry.content:
Executive Summary

Chicago’s fire code requires annual inspection of commercial and high-occupancy buildings (#fire-code). An October 2025 audit by the city’s Inspector General reviewed 59,313 records (27,491 buildings plus 31,822 tenant spaces) in the Fire Prevention Bureau’s database (#fpb-count) and found that only 16.8% received their annual inspection in the year before the audit’s data pull (#inspect-rate); 47.1% had gone five or more years without one, some not in decades (#half-uninspected). Chicago’s own fire deaths are near historic lows (#chicago-fire-deaths), so this is not a body count. It is a mandated safety system running at a fraction of its required rate, the kind of fragmented oversight that, in its worst form, produced disasters like Grenfell Tower and Ghost Ship in other cities (#grenfell), (#ghost-ship).

Three contributions follow. First, a building inventory of the kind the OIG recommended and that CFD’s response treated as the Department of Buildings’ responsibility rather than its own (#cfd-response). From public violation, permit, and 311 records I classified roughly 81,351 Chicago buildings into the use types the annual-inspection mandate targets (#inventory), about 3x the 27,491 buildings OIG was able to review (an approximation from permit-text keywords, not a validated register; see Finding 2). Of those, roughly 40,722 have zero building-violation records (#black-holes), and 47,227 are flagged across five risk buckets (#total-flagged). Second, a diagnosis of why inspection alone doesn’t reduce hazards: an enforcement model that imposes fines but rarely collects them. Third, a legislative path from the new Healthy Homes working group to combined inspection with stronger lien enforcement.

The gap is throughput, and systems are the tractable lever. NYC’s fire inspectors conduct more than 250,000 inspections a year with about 400 inspectors, roughly 12 per inspector per week; Chicago’s 9,971 annual inspections across an inspection workforce of 62 to 89 work out to about 2 to 3 per inspector per week (#throughput). The counts are not perfectly comparable (NYC’s includes re-inspections), but the gap is large on any reading. It is not purely a headcount problem: NYC itself carries a 49,834-inspection backlog and says it needs both more inspectors and the automated targeting and routing it has not fully deployed (#nyc-backlog). A real building inventory, risk-based targeting, and route optimization are what Chicago lacks entirely, and what the tool here supplies.

Inspection alone doesn’t fix buildings. Enforcement does. Chicago summons the person to an administrative hearing, and about 68% of building-violation cases end without the owner engaging: roughly 24% are default judgments and 44% are cases the city itself drops before hearing (#non-engage). The result is $827M in imposed building fines (#fines-total), little of it collected, against $3.1B in uncollected debt across the whole administrative-hearing system (#debt-hearing). NYC’s data shows property-attached charges collect far better than person-attached penalties (the two are not a clean comparison), and its budget office estimates material gains from making penalties lienable (#nyc-rates), (#nyc-ibo). Illinois already gives Chicago lien and receivership authority (#peer-gaps); the gap is systematic use. And even when inspections happen, five departments hold separate authority over fire, structure, lead, environmental, and habitability conditions in the same buildings (#five-depts), so an inspector standing in an in-scope building who sees a non-fire hazard cannot cite it.

The economics support a pilot, not a budgeted revenue line. A lean Year-1 pilot runs an estimated $410K, more realistically $0.5-0.8M fully loaded (#impl-cost). A combined inspection authority with stronger lien enforcement could plausibly raise gross revenue on the order of tens of millions a year, with a wide modeled range (roughly $29M to $118M/yr incremental gross, before recurring operating costs of $2.5-6M/yr) (#net-benefit), (#scale-up-cost). These are upper-bound scenarios anchored to peer programs operating today (LA collects $50-60M/yr from licensing and carries a surplus (#peer-fees), (#fee-surplus)) and to Chicago’s own history: the city imposed $62-75M/yr in building fines in 2010-2012 versus ~$17M today (#fines-annual). The case for a pilot rests on that verified history and the inspection gap, not on the model’s top end.

The ask. Three actions close the gap: adopt the risk scoring tool for inspection prioritization (no legislation needed); pass a combined-inspection ordinance creating a Building Safety Inspector credential (a cross-department role that has to be negotiated with the affected unions and drafted against the current code (#bsi-constraints)); and use Chicago’s existing lien and receivership authority systematically for building violations. The Healthy Homes Ordinance (passed March 18, 2026) (#healthy-homes) already chartered the working group this fits. The tool is open source and built from public data; CFD’s practitioner feedback is what would turn it from a data-grounded prototype into an operational queue.

Background

What the law requires

Chicago’s fire code mandates that the Fire Prevention Bureau (FPB) conduct annual inspections of all commercial, institutional, and high-occupancy properties. The OIG’s October 2025 audit reviewed 27,491 buildings and 31,822 tenant spaces (59,313 inspection records in total) in FPB’s database (#fpb-count). OIG limited its review to records with at least one inspection on file in the prior 12 years; records with no inspection were excluded as potentially invalid. The actual mandated universe is therefore unknown and almost certainly larger than 59,313.

What the OIG found

The Chicago Inspector General published an audit in October 2025 documenting gaps in fire prevention inspections:

  • Only 15.8% of buildings and 17.7% of tenant spaces received their annual inspection (16.8% combined) (#inspect-rate)
  • 49.4% of buildings and 45.1% of tenant spaces haven’t been inspected in five or more years (47.1% combined) (#half-uninspected); some not in decades
  • FPB had 89 budgeted positions in 2021-2024; in its response, CFD said staffing fell from 156 budgeted positions (2000) to 86 (2025), 62 of them assigned to inspection duties (#staff-cut)
  • $1.1M in re-inspection fees went uncollected over 10 years (only 13.2% collection rate) (#fee-uncollected)
  • Fire suppression system testing compliance: sprinklers 73.7%, fire pumps 79.6%, standpipes 77.8% (#suppress-test)
  • Median time between violation finding and re-check: 5.2 months (#recheck-delay)
  • Responsibility for maintaining a complete building inventory was contested between CFD and DOB
  • Missing violation dates and disposition statuses in CFD’s own records
  • CFD destroyed paper inspection reports without approval from Cook County Local Records Commission

CFD’s response

The OIG made four recommendations: that CFD (1) work with the Department of Technology and Innovation (DTI) and the Department of Buildings (DOB) to identify a complete and accurate inventory of buildings subject to annual inspection, (2) establish procedures for all required inspections, (3) create a progress-monitoring process, and (4) standardize recordkeeping (#cfd-response).

CFD largely disagreed with the inventory recommendation. In its formal response it took the position that the official register of buildings is DOB’s responsibility, not CFD’s, citing MCC 14A-6-602.4, and that “CFD stands ready to participate in any improvement efforts DOB elects to pursue” (#cfd-response). On several of the monitoring and testing recommendations, CFD responded that its third-party compliance engine (the Brycer system, which the audit itself calls “The Compliance Engine”) already issues the deficiency notices the OIG sought, so in CFD’s view “no corrective action could be taken.” Whether that system actually closes the gaps the audit documents is a fair question, and exactly the kind of question CFD’s own practitioners are best placed to answer. What the audit establishes regardless is the underlying gap: there is no validated, shared inventory of the buildings subject to annual inspection, and most of those that OIG could review are not being inspected on schedule. This is a recurring pattern across Chicago departments: the OIG identifies a gap and recommends action; the department disagrees or points elsewhere; the gap persists. The tools described here are meant to give the working group a concrete way to break that cycle.

Findings

Finding 1: Chicago’s inspection throughput runs far below comparable cities

With about 17% compliance (15.8% of buildings, 17.7% of tenant spaces) and a small inspection workforce, the natural question is whether the gap is a staffing problem or a systems problem. The honest answer is some of both, and the comparison to NYC shows why the tractable near-term lever is systems.

City Inspectors Inspections/yr Annual compliance Source
NYC (FDNY) ~400 250,000+ not published (#nyc-inspection)
Chicago (CFD) 86 budgeted, 62 inspecting 9,971 16.8% (#inspect-rate)
San Francisco – – 93% of apartments (2017) (#sf-inspection)
Portland ~13 companies – ~100% biennial (#portland-inspection)
NFPA workload guideline (1982) – 500-600 / inspector – (#nfpa-benchmark)

The clearest sourced comparison is raw throughput. NYC’s Bureau of Fire Prevention has roughly 400 inspectors and conducts more than 250,000 inspections a year (#nyc-inspection), about 12 per inspector per week. Chicago completed 9,971 annual inspections in the 12 months before the OIG’s data pull, 16.8% of the 59,313 records OIG reviewed (#throughput). Spread across FPB’s inspection workforce (86 budgeted positions in 2025, of which CFD says 62 are assigned to inspection duties; 89 budgeted during the 2021-2022 window OIG measured), that is on the order of 2 to 3 inspections per inspector per week, with on-duty fire companies performing a further share on top of FPB’s own work (#throughput). The two counts are not perfectly commensurable: NYC’s total includes re-inspections while Chicago’s compliance count excludes them, so this comparison understates Chicago’s total activity and, if anything, overstates the gap. Even after that caveat the gap is large, on the order of four to five times under any reasonable choice of denominator.

This is a throughput figure, not a verdict on individual inspectors. It is an organizational coverage rate that folds in travel, paperwork, and scheduling overhead, derived from annual totals rather than observed individual output (#throughput). Read that way it measures the same quantity NYC’s number does, and Chicago’s is a small fraction of it.

Two cautions keep this honest. First, the compliance data is a snapshot: the 16.8% covers the 12 months ending November 2022, when OIG pulled FPB’s records (#fpb-count). CFD attributes part of the shortfall to the COVID-era suspension of in-service company inspections, which it resumed in 2024. But 47.1% of the reviewed records had gone five or more years without an inspection as of that November 2022 pull (#half-uninspected), so most of the backlog predates the pandemic; COVID deepened a gap that already existed. Second, NYC is not a picture of full compliance. Its own auditors found 49,834 overdue annual inspections, reported that FDNY estimated needing 30% more inspectors to clear the backlog, and noted FDNY “did not implement automated inspections and optimized routing as intended” (#nyc-backlog). That cuts two ways: added capacity is part of any real fix, and the inventory, risk targeting, and routing that NYC has only partly deployed are exactly the systems with the most room to run. The 1982 NFPA workload guideline of 500-600 inspections per inspector per year (roughly 10-12 a week) is the historical yardstick (#nfpa-benchmark); Chicago runs at about a fifth to a third of it (#nfpa-pct), though NFPA has since replaced fixed productivity numbers with a community-risk-based methodology. At even the low end of that old guideline, the same 86 inspectors would complete roughly 45,000 inspections a year, about three-quarters of the records OIG reviewed, instead of one-sixth (#nfpa-coverage).

Finding 2: A public-data inventory finds roughly 3x the buildings OIG could review

The most basic tool other cities use is a building inventory: which buildings exist, what condition are they in, and when were they last inspected. The OIG recommended one. It has not been built.

Using three public datasets (1.99M building violations, permits, and 311 service complaints), I constructed an inventory of 340,573 Chicago buildings with a public footprint in any of those sources, then classified each by use type from its permit work-description text. Of the 340,573, roughly 81,351 fall into the use types the annual-inspection mandate targets (commercial, industrial, multi-unit residential, and assembly) (#inventory). That is roughly 3x the 27,491 buildings OIG was able to review (#fpb-count). The comparison is not exact: OIG reviewed a curated sample (records with at least one inspection in a 12-year window), and the 81,351 is an approximation built from keyword classification of permit text, not a validated building register. But the order of magnitude is the OIG’s central operational finding made visible: the count of in-scope buildings visible in routine public data is far larger than the set FPB could show the auditors.

How solid is the 81,351? The use-type classification is approximate. It is assigned from keywords in each building’s permit work-description text, so a single-family home with a permit to “erect a 2-car frame garage” can be tagged industrial, and the pipeline applies no building-height filter even though the fire-code mandate turns partly on height and occupancy (#fire-code). The industrial category (41,740 buildings) is almost certainly inflated by this. The 81,351 should be read as a use-type approximation that brackets the true in-scope universe, not a precise count; validating it against the county assessor’s building-characteristics data is the obvious next step before the figure carries any load-bearing weight. What the approximation establishes is directional and robust to the classification error: the in-scope stock is a multiple of what FPB has on file, which is the gap the OIG flagged.

Of the 81,351 OIG-scope buildings, 47,227 (58%) fall into at least one of five risk buckets (#total-flagged):

Bucket OIG-scope flagged All use types What It Identifies
Black Holes ~40,700 ~40,700 Zero building-violation records, OIG-scope building type (#black-holes)
Chronic Failures ~2,900 ~9,400 5+ severe violations, still unresolved (#chronic)
Ticking Clocks ~1,600 ~6,800 Severe history + 10yr+ inspection gap (#ticking)
Community Alerts ~1,700 ~8,400 2+ 311 complaints in 3 years (#alerts)
Open & Forgotten ~2,300 ~11,400 10+ open violations + 10yr+ gap (#forgotten)
Total unique ~47,000 ~69,000 Black Holes is OIG-scope by design; other buckets include both OIG-scope and non-OIG-scope buildings (#total-flagged)

The Black Holes bucket flags OIG-scope buildings with zero building-violation records in the public city datasets used here. These datasets contain no CFD fire-inspection records at all, so a zero here means no public evidence of attention (no violation, and the building reached the inventory only through a permit or 311 record), not a confirmed absence of any inspection ever performed. The OIG audit’s separate finding (that ~83% of mandated buildings are not receiving annual inspections) strongly implies a large share of these are genuinely uninspected, but the bucket is defined by the absence of a violation record, not by a confirmed absence of inspection. A building that was inspected without producing a violation could appear here.

These counts are approximate and shift slightly as the city updates its data. The order of magnitude and relative proportions are stable. See bucket_summary.csv for exact counts from the most recent run.

The tool also generates daily route plans for inspectors. Given a starting location and a number of stops, it selects the highest-priority buildings across all five categories and orders them to minimize travel time between stops.

Finding 3: Building fines are imposed but rarely collected

A risk scoring tool tells inspectors where to go. But inspection alone doesn’t fix buildings. Enforcement does. Chicago’s current enforcement model has a structural weakness that other cities have already addressed.

Chicago imposes fines through administrative hearings where the person is summoned. In 2023-2024, roughly 68% of building violation cases ended without the owner engaging. About 24% were default judgments (respondent never appears, average fine $2,932 imposed but rarely collected). Another 44% were non-suits (case dropped entirely, average fine $10) (#non-engage). Judgments are entered against the person, not the property. When a building is sold, the buyer gets a clean slate.

The scale of uncollected debt reflects how long non-engagement has accumulated. Three different totals are visible in public data, each measuring something different: building-related fines alone total $827M imposed since 2006 (#fines-total); the administrative hearing system as a whole (all departments, not just buildings) carries $3.1B in uncollected debt (#debt-hearing); citywide unpaid fines, fees, and debts (including water bills, parking tickets, and other obligations beyond the hearing system) total $8.2B (#debt-total). These three do not nest simply: $827M is imposed (collected-or-not), $3.1B is uncollected only within admin hearings, $8.2B is uncollected across all city collection systems. They are shown together to convey the scale at which non-collection has accumulated, not to sum.

Fire code violations are nearly absent from the hearing system. Only about 30 cases linked to fire prevention appear among 829,000+ admin hearing records, all tagged as “Buildings” department rather than “Fire” (#cfd-absent). The only documented CFD enforcement revenue is roughly $14,500/yr in re-check fees at a 13.2% collection rate (OIG).

Other cities attach fines to the property (#peer-gaps):

City Mechanism How It Works
NYC ERP / AEP / 7A City repairs hazards, costs become property lien. Worst buildings get court-appointed administrator.
LA REAP Tenants pay rent to city escrow until violations are fixed. Owners lose rental income.
DC Proactive inspections + liens Violations become property liens. Collected at sale or refinancing.
Chicago Admin hearings Owner summoned. ~68% never engage (default or non-suit). Fines go uncollected.

Today’s enforcement level is not a baseline. It is a departure from historical norms.

In 2010-2012, Chicago imposed $62-75M/yr in building fines across 65,000-68,000 cases (#fines-annual). In 2013, the Code Enforcement budget was cut by 29% (#enforcement-cut) and DOB priorities shifted toward permit streamlining. Citywide, 2,150+ vacant positions were eliminated as part of broader budget restructuring (#2012-budget).

The effects were immediate. Cases filed dropped 30% and average fines dropped 36% (#enforcement-cut). The non-suit rate (cases dropped before hearing) rose from 26% to 37% (#fines-annual). A 2018 OIG audit found a backlog of 5,000+ open complaints dating back to 2013 (#oig-complaints). Enforcement has not recovered. Today’s $17M/yr is 57% below the pre-2013 average of ~$40M/yr, even as case counts are starting to return (#fines-annual).

NYC’s own data points the same way. Person-attached DOB penalties collect at about 28%; property-attached water and sewer charges collect at roughly 80% (#nyc-rates). The two are not a clean controlled comparison: water and sewer charges collect well partly because they carry utility-shutoff leverage and ride into tax-lien sales, mechanisms a building fine lacks. But the direction matches what NYC’s own Independent Budget Office concluded when it recommended making DOB penalties lienable, estimating on the order of +$100M/yr in additional collection (#nyc-ibo).

Finding 4: Five departments, five legal authorities, one building

Even with better targeting and enforcement, the inspection system itself is fragmented. Five separate departments hold legal authority over distinct conditions in the same buildings (fire, structure, lead, environmental, habitability), each operating under its own Municipal Code chapter, with no mechanism to share findings or combine visits (#five-depts). The fragmentation here is in legal authority, not necessarily in observed site visits: I did not measure how often all five departments actually send overlapping inspections to the same address. What is clear is that, by code, no inspector currently has cross-department authority, so any one visit can address only one slice of building safety.

Department Inspects Legal Authority
CFD Fire exits, sprinklers, alarms MCC 15-4 (Fire Code, Title 14F)
DOB Building code, structural MCC Title 14A (building code)
CDPH Lead paint, mold, environmental MCC 7-4, 7-28
BACP Business-license conditions MCC Title 4
DOB/Housing Habitability, heat, water MCC 5-12 and building property-maintenance provisions

The chapter citations above are a high-level map, not drafting language: the 2019-2022 recodification moved the building and fire codes into Titles 14A and 14F, and some conditions (habitability in particular) are enforced through housing-court and private-tenant remedies rather than a single inspection chapter, so a combined-inspection ordinance would have to be drafted by the Law Department against the current codified provisions (#five-depts).

A fire inspector standing in a daycare, shelter, or single-room-occupancy building, all within the annual-inspection scope, who sees peeling lead paint or black mold has no legal authority to cite either. Most of an inspector’s time is spent traveling between buildings. If an inspector is already on-site, adding checklists from other departments costs little additional time. The added training is modest, though one row carries a state-licensing caveat:

Checklist Training Items
Fire safety Existing Exits, detectors, sprinklers, extinguishers
Housing 2 days Heat, water, pests, windows, wiring
Lead paint 1 day Visual screen and referral only (citable lead inspection requires IDPH licensure)
Environmental 1 day Mold, standing water, ventilation

These departments employ roughly 140 inspectors whose work falls within the scope a combined Building Safety Inspector credential would cover (#pool-size). “Overlapping” here means overlapping legal scope (fire/structure/lead/environmental/habitability conditions in the same buildings), not a measured count of duplicate site visits.

CFD has 62 actively conducting inspections (of 86 total FPB positions). The Department of Buildings has approximately 40 building and construction inspectors (31 plus 9 supervisors), with another 26 inspector-titled positions in non-overlapping specialties (elevators, boilers, plumbing, electrical). CDPH has roughly 39 building-related staff across building inspection, sanitation, environmental, and supervisory roles.

Cross-training this existing pool is the core of the proposal: create a “Building Safety Inspector” credential, paired with an ordinance recognizing cross-department inspection authority. These are checklists, not specialized engineering (#cross-train).

Three implementation constraints have to be named up front (#bsi-constraints). First, FPB’s inspectors are sworn firefighters in a bargaining unit (Local 2); changing their duties is a mandatory subject of collective bargaining under the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act, so a combined-inspection role has to be negotiated, not simply assigned by ordinance. Second, a new job classification is created through the city’s classification plan and the annual appropriation ordinance, not by amending the substantive Municipal Code chapters that define each inspection authority; the credential and the cross-authority ordinance are separate legislative acts. Third, lead-hazard inspection in Illinois is a state-licensed activity (an IDPH-approved course, a state exam, and annual licensure), so the one-day lead module yields a visual screen and a referral, not citable lead-inspection authority; any environmental checklist with its own licensing regime carries the same caveat. None of these blocks combining inspections, and peer cities have done it, but each is a step the proposal has to budget and plan for rather than wave past.

The Healthy Homes Ordinance (passed City Council March 18, 2026) creates a working group to design a proactive rental inspection system (#healthy-homes). That working group’s mandate crosses department boundaries. It needs a building inventory, risk-based prioritization, and route planning. The tool described here provides all three.

Finding 5: The economics favor action

Can a combined inspection authority pay for itself? The peer city evidence and Chicago’s own historical enforcement data suggest it can.

Phase 1, pilot implementation cost (Year 1):

Item Cost Notes
Cross-training $190K 86 inspectors x 1 week x $114K avg salary / 52 wks. Salary time only; one-time.
Program design & pilot $75K Curriculum, certification, pilot in 2-3 wards. One-time.
Program coordinator $110K 1 FTE to manage rollout, track metrics. Recurring, not one-time.
Data integration $35K Dashboard, city IT connection. Tool itself is open source.
Phase 1 total ~$410K (#impl-cost)

The $410K is a deliberately lean pilot figure and a lower bound. It prices cross-training as straight salary time for the 86 FPB inspectors only; it excludes employee fringe (typically 30-40% on top of salary), overtime or backfill for the inspection week lost to training, and the eventual cost of training the roughly 54 additional DOB and CDPH inspectors in the combined pool. A fully loaded Phase 1 is more realistically in the $0.5-0.8M range, and the coordinator line is recurring rather than one-time (#impl-cost). The cross-training count also inherits the 86-vs-62 question from Finding 1: if only ~62 FPB inspectors are active, the training line shrinks, but so does the throughput base the pilot is trying to lift. Phase 1 covers pilot activities only (cross-training, routing the tool through city IT, a bounded pilot in 2-3 wards); it does not cover the systems and enforcement staffing required for Phase 2 (combined-inspection ordinance) or Phase 3 (property-lien enforcement).

Phase 2-3 scale-up costs (if ordinances pass):

Item One-time Recurring Notes
Legal drafting (ordinance, 5 MCC chapters) $100-300K n/a Internal law dept or external counsel
IT build beyond pilot dashboard $500K-2M $200-500K/yr Inspection queue, mobile inspector app, integrations
Collections infrastructure n/a $1-3M/yr Staff + systems for 4-6x fine volume
Lien administration n/a $500K-1M/yr Property-attached enforcement workflow
Hearing / appeals capacity n/a $500K-1.5M/yr Volume increase handling
Phase 2-3 total (range) $600K-2.3M one-time ~$2.5-6M/yr (#scale-up-cost)

These are planning-grade estimates based on comparable municipal IT and enforcement program scopes; actual costs depend on scope, staffing model, and procurement path, and would be refined during the pilot. The recurring Phase 2-3 operating cost ($2.5-6M/yr) is the figure that needs to be subtracted from the gross revenue projections below to convert “projected incremental gross revenue” into a true net fiscal benefit.

For context, the city spends $83M per year on police tort judgments alone (#cpd-tort). Phase 1 costs less than 0.5% of that. Even the high end of Phase 2-3 recurring cost ($6M/yr) would be less than 10% of that single line item.

Capacity gains from the tool alone (no legislative change required):

  • Route optimization: literature suggests +20-40% inspections/day in comparable field service contexts (#route-opt)
  • Risk prioritization (buckets): proactive targeting literature suggests +25-50% violations found per visit (#risk-target)
  • Blind spot elimination: more than 40,000 buildings with no inspection-generated public record enter the queue

Current throughput is roughly 190 inspections per week organization-wide (#throughput-now). At 50% of the 1982 NFPA workload guideline, the same 86 inspectors could reach roughly 430 per week; at the full guideline, roughly 860 per week (#nfpa-cap). These are capacity illustrations against a superseded guideline, not forecasts.

Revenue model: gross uplift only, before recurring operating costs (modeled scenarios based on city data, OIG audit, and peer city actuals):

The figures below are projected incremental gross revenue, not net benefit. They subtract today’s revenue baseline but do not subtract the recurring operating costs of running a combined authority (collections staff, legal process, lien administration, billing, hearings, appeals, and enforcement overhead). Treat them as upper-bound revenue scenarios that establish whether the proposal is plausibly self-funding and worth a pilot, not as a hard fiscal forecast a city budget office could book.

Current building enforcement fines average ~$17M/yr imposed (2023-2025 average). That is 57% below the pre-2013 average of ~$40M/yr and far below the 2010-2012 peak of $62-75M/yr (#fines-annual). Those higher levels were achieved with fewer tools and no risk-based targeting.

Actual Chicago collection rates are unknown; no collections-level payment data is published. The estimated 28-34% range uses the NYC IBO person-attached analogue (28%) as the lower bound and the inverse of the ~68% non-engagement rate as the upper bound. At those rates, current enforcement revenue is an estimated ~$5-6M (#fines-annual).

Every figure except the “Today” column is a modeled estimate, not an observed value. The collection-rate inputs are the largest single source of uncertainty: they are NYC analogues, not measured Chicago rates. The “Tool Only” fines-imposed range ($25-35M) applies a route-optimization range (+20-40%) (#route-opt) and a risk-targeting range (+25-50%) (#risk-target) drawn from the literature, not from a measured Chicago pilot. The “Combined Authority” and “Combined + Liens” fines-imposed range ($60-100M) uses the pre-2013 historical level ($62-75M/yr) as the lower bound; the upper bound is a scenario, not a calibrated forecast. Licensing-fee revenue in the peer cities is structured as cost recovery: it funds the inspection program rather than adding net general revenue, so that row should be read as program funding, not surplus. The suppression-fee line is a range because the $3.4M end assumes full compliance and collection against an actual ~$14,500/yr today (#suppress-rev). The “Incremental gross uplift” row is a gross revenue projection; recurring operating costs of a combined authority are not modeled, so it should not be read as net fiscal benefit. See Notes (#net-benefit), (#per-inspector) for input assumptions and sensitivity.

Backlog recovery (estimate, not forecast): $3.1B in existing admin hearing debt (#debt-hearing). At an estimated 5-20% recovery via property liens, that would be a one-time $155-620M (#backlog). The 5-20% range is a planning estimate; actual recovery depends on debt age, debtor solvency, lien implementation costs, and political will, none of which are modeled here.

Finding 6: Peer cities have already solved these problems

The revenue projections above are modeled estimates. The underlying programs are not hypothetical; they are operating today. Methodology

Data sources

Three Socrata datasets form the building inventory:

  • Building Violations: 22u3-xenr (1.99M rows, 1M+ since 2006)
  • Building Permits: ydr8-5enu (65K+/year since 2006)
  • 311 Service Requests: v6vf-nfxy (filtered to fire/building types)

Enforcement analysis uses Ordinance Violations: awqx-tuwv (829,000+ records). Inspector staffing from Budget Positions: wd4x-2xf8.

Pipeline

Step Script What It Does
1 01_fetch.py Downloads 3 datasets from Socrata
2 02_normalize.py Cleans, deduplicates, canonicalizes Chicago addresses
3 03_build_inventory.py Joins datasets into building inventory (1 row/building) (#inventory)
4 04_score.py Assigns buildings to 5 risk buckets with within-bucket ranking
5 05_report.py Generates INSPECTION_PRIORITY_REPORT.md organized by bucket
6 06_route.py Optimizes inspector routes (haversine distance + OR-Tools TSP)

Scoring design: buckets over composite scores

A single composite risk score creates surveillance bias: frequently inspected buildings accumulate violations and score high, while never-inspected buildings score zero. The OIG’s core concern (~49,000 uninspected buildings) would rank last under a composite score. Buckets separate fundamentally different problems (never-inspected vs. chronic failure vs. community concern) with tailored ranking criteria within each bucket.

Compliance-first, not prediction-first

Existing fire risk tools (Firebird/Atlanta, CMU Metro21/Pittsburgh, SF Brigade) try to predict which buildings will have fires. CFD needs something different: “Which of my 59,313 buildings should my 86 inspectors visit tomorrow?” This is an inspection gap + risk factor scoring problem, not a fire occurrence prediction problem. Compliance-first scoring doesn’t require fire incident data (which Chicago doesn’t publish on Socrata). It uses violation history, inspection dates, building characteristics, and 311 complaints to rank overdue buildings by risk.

Denominators are conservative

Every percentage here computed against OIG’s 59,313 reviewed records understates the true gap. OIG narrowed its review to buildings and tenant spaces with at least one inspection on file in a 12-year window; records with no inspection were excluded as potentially invalid, because FPB has no validated building inventory (that absence is OIG’s central operational finding). The full mandated universe is therefore unknown and almost certainly larger than 59,313. When the figures here say 16.8% compliance, 2 to 3 inspections per inspector per week, or ~75% projected coverage at the 1982 NFPA guideline, the underlying state of the world is at least this bad, and likely worse. The 81,351 OIG-scope buildings visible in public data (Finding 2) is one indicator of how much larger the real universe may be.

Data freshness and what is committed

Of the pipeline artifacts the Notes reference, only route.csv is committed to this report directory. The larger intermediates (scored_buildings.csv, bucket_*.csv, bucket_summary.csv) are excluded by .gitignore to keep the repository light and are regenerated by running the pipeline (see Reproducibility). The bucket counts cited in the Notes are recorded in the committed Hydra run logs under runs/ (for example runs/04_score_2026-03-28_18-17-30/), produced on 2026-03-28 from the Socrata datasets listed above. So the grep/wc commands in the Notes run against a freshly generated scored_buildings.csv, not a file already in the published tree; a reader who wants a bucket count without re-running the pipeline can read it from the run log. Socrata refreshes continuously, so a fresh run produces slightly different counts; the order of magnitude and relative proportions are stable.

Validation

7 buildings were checked against the live Socrata API. Raw violation counts matched exactly for all 7 (#api-check). Pipeline counts for each bucket are checked by automated tests against broad ranges to accommodate Socrata data refreshes; the subset of tests that read pipeline-output CSVs are skipped on a clean checkout (those files are gitignored) and run only after the pipeline is regenerated, while the Socrata-query and derived-math tests run against live data with no regeneration needed.

Throughput methodology note: The per-inspector throughput in Finding 1 (roughly 2 to 3 inspections per inspector per week) is a derived organizational proxy (annual inspections divided by workforce and weeks), not a directly observed per-inspector measurement. It reflects an effective coverage rate that includes systemic overhead (travel, paperwork, scheduling) and folds in inspections performed by on-duty fire companies as well as FPB. The comparison to NYC’s ~12/week is directional: NYC’s count includes re-inspections while Chicago’s counts only first annual-compliance inspections, so the gap is real but its exact size is uncertain (#throughput).

entry.title: A 75-Word Limit Shouldn’t Take Five Tries

link.title: A 75-Word Limit Shouldn’t Take Five Tries

entry.content:
Ask a language model to answer a patient’s question from their medical record. Simple enough. Now add constraints: ground every claim in a specific sentence from the clinical note. Keep it under 75 words. Use past tense for events during hospitalization, present tense for prognosis. Match the style of a clinician writing for a lay reader.

Each of these instructions is straightforward on its own. Stack them together and the model starts failing in ways that standard evaluation metrics don’t capture.

The 75-word problem

We built a system for the ArchEHR-QA 2026 shared task, which evaluates grounded question answering from electronic health records. The task requires a model to identify which sentences in a clinical note support the answer, generate a natural-language response under 75 words, and align each answer sentence to its evidence.

The simplest constraint was the hardest to enforce. On the development set, 85.9% of outputs met all format and length requirements on the first attempt. On the test set, that dropped to 64.3%. Word count violations accounted for 95% of all test errors. Not citation errors. Not format errors. The model couldn’t count to 75.

We fixed this with an iterative correction loop: when an output violated a constraint, we told the model exactly what was wrong and let it retry, up to five times. The loop achieved 100% compliance on both sets. But the fact that it was necessary at all is the point. A model that needs five attempts to meet a word limit it was given in the original prompt is not following instructions. It’s being corrected into compliance.

What the metrics missed

The compliance loop solved the format problem. It did not solve the style problem.

Our system matched clinician-authored answers on word count (72.7 vs. 73.5) and sentence count (4.45 vs. 4.75). Neither difference was statistically significant. By the most obvious measures, the outputs looked like clinician writing.

They weren’t. We computed 45 linguistic features across six categories and compared model outputs to clinician referencesWe used paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons across 45 features.. Eight features diverged significantly. The model wrote text that was 3.2 Flesch-Kincaid grade levels harder to readFlesch-Kincaid Grade Level estimates the US school grade needed to understand a text. The clinician reference averaged grade 10.7. The model averaged 13.9, roughly college level.. It used longer words, fewer function words, and produced denser, more noun-heavy prose. The writing read like a medical textbook, not like a clinician explaining a result to a patient.

These answers are intended for patients. A response that is factually correct, properly grounded, and within the word limit can still fail its purpose if the patient can’t understand it. The standard evaluation metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, MEDCON) did not flag this gap. Length matched. Style didn’t.

The retry loop repaired what the benchmark could see. It did not repair what the communication task actually required.

More instructions, worse results

The natural question is why. The model was explicitly instructed to write in plain language. It was given style guidance, tense rules, and a word limit. Why did it follow the word limit (eventually) but not the register?

Some researchers call the failure mode “cognitive overload.” LLMs do not have cognition. What happens is better described as constraint interference: the model satisfies whichever instruction is most explicitly reinforced and underperforms on the rest. Word count is easy to verify and correct. Register is not. In our results, that asymmetry is exact: every word-count failure triggered a correction attempt; no equivalent mechanism existed to detect or retry a register failure.

You can split the task. That doesn’t solve the problem.

We tested whether separating the competing objectives would help. After the submission deadline, we built a three-step rewrite variant: (1) generate an unconstrained answer grounded in the evidence, (2) rewrite it for clinical register, (3) enforce the word limit as a separate call.

The decomposed pipeline reduced the linguistic distance to the clinician reference from 0.519 to 0.381 and improved the answer generation score (Subtask 3 Overall) by approximately two points on the development set. Readability moved closer to clinician levels. The cost: 9.5x latency and a three-stage orchestrated pipeline in place of a single model call.

That cost is the point. The improvement didn’t come from a better model or a smarter prompt. It came from decomposing the problem, routing each subproblem to a separate call, and engineering the handoffs. At some point you’re not using a language model to generate answers. You’re building a scaffold around one to compensate for what it can’t do reliably. The benchmark credit belongs to the pipeline, not the model.

64.3% is the real number

Our system achieved 100% compliance after correction. That sounds like success. But 100% compliance after five attempts is not the same as 100% compliance on the first attempt. The first number means the scaffold works. The second number means the model works. On the test set, the model’s first-pass compliance was 64.3%. That is the real number.

In clinical settings, the tolerance for errors approaches zero. If a system cannot demonstrate near-zero error rates on simple, verifiable constraints like word count, it cannot be trusted with harder, less verifiable ones like reading level, tone, and clinical accuracy. The easy constraints are the lower bound. If the model fails there, everything above it is suspect.

The workarounds exist. Decompose, correct, verify, repeat. Each layer of scaffolding is an admission that the model alone is not reliable enough. When the benchmark reports performance on a system like this, the credit belongs to the scaffold, not to the model. In clinical applications, the difference between a reliable model and a reliable scaffold is the difference that matters.
entry.summary: We asked a language model to answer patient questions under simple constraints. It matched the word count. It didn't match the writing.

entry.title: Hiring When Every Resume Looks the Same

link.title: Hiring When Every Resume Looks the Same

entry.content:
73 people applied for two research assistant positions in my center. Most of their resumes looked the same. Everyone knew Python. Everyone listed machine learning, NLP, and deep learning. Everyone had a project or two on GitHub. Reading 73 applications where every candidate claims fluency in everything is not a screening process. It’s noise.

And that’s before you account for AI tools. Every one of these candidates had access to AI tools. The floor on what someone can produce has risen. The traditional approach (screen resumes, then run candidates through four or five rounds of interviews to figure out what’s real) doesn’t scale when the resumes all look the same and the submitted work might not be theirs.

I wasn’t evaluating anyone’s ability to generate code. I was evaluating critical judgment. I needed people who could work in an environment where the hardest part isn’t writing code. It’s deciding what to do when the data is ambiguous, the requirements are underspecified, and a quiet mistake compounds for months before anyone notices. That’s not something you can evaluate with a resume screen or a puzzle question.

So I designed something different.

Messy data, real decisions, blitz interview

I gave candidates two intentionally messy CSV files and a prediction task: hospital readmission. Dirty dates. Vitals recorded after discharge. Extreme values. Missing fields. A patient ID that appeared in one file but not the other. 24 hours. AI tools welcome, as long as candidates could take full ownership of what they submitted.

The point wasn’t the prediction. It was the mess. Every dataset had decisions buried in it. What to do about the post-discharge vitals. How to handle the mismatched IDs. Whether to impute or drop. There was no right answer to most of these. I wanted to see how candidates navigated that.

I code-reviewed every submission. I wasn’t checking whether scripts ran. I was reading for judgment: did they notice the leakage? Did they document their choices? Did they handle the ambiguity or pretend it wasn’t there?

The funnel: 73 to 4

73 eligible. 45 after requiring a referral. 35 submitted. 14 showed enough judgment in the code review to earn a live round.

Then 4.

The live interview was 30 minutes, and the questioning was targeted at ownership. Walk me through your code. Why did you make this choice? Now make a small change.

This was the most informative step in the entire process. The most significant factor in my decisions was the gap between a candidate’s stated proficiency and their ability to solve problems independently in the live round. Several candidates turned in polished, well-structured work and then couldn’t walk through a design choice or make a targeted modification to their own code.

The work looked like theirs. The understanding wasn’t.

The real filter

The take-home filtered for judgment. The blitz filtered for something more basic: did they actually know what they submitted? Some candidates who turned in clean, well-reasoned code couldn’t explain basic concepts in conversation. Some couldn’t write a few lines of Python to filter a dataframe when asked to make a small change live.

The ownership gap matters because the work is research. A pipeline the author doesn’t understand is a finding that can’t be trusted. A silent error isn’t a bug you patch next sprint. It’s months of wasted work or a wrong conclusion that gets published. The accountability is higher, and there’s no shortcut around understanding what your code actually does.

The difference isn’t between people who use AI tools and people who don’t. It’s between people who recognize the limitations of these tools and work around them, and people who follow their output blindly.

A Harvard/BCG study found that when AI gave plausible but wrong answers, consultants who trusted it without critical judgment performed worse than those with no AI at all. The ones who recognized the limits were far more productive. That’s who I was hiring for.
entry.summary: 73 applicants, two positions, and every candidate had access to AI.
